nameStory: The Indo-Pacific House Gecko gets its name from its vast natural range across the Indo-Pacific region, stretching from South Asia through the Pacific islands. It's called a 'house gecko' because these little lizards love to live in and around human buildings, where they hunt insects attracted to lights. You might also hear it called Garnot's house gecko, named after the French naturalist Prosper Garnot who first described it scientifically.
description: The Indo-Pacific House Gecko is a small, tropical lizard that occasionally shows up in New England as an accidental stowaway in shipping containers or imported goods. These geckos are quite small, growing only 4-5 inches long from nose to tail tip. They have the amazing ability to change color from dark gray or brown during the day to pale, almost see-through white at night. With their large eyes, sticky toe pads, and soft, bumpy skin, they look like tiny dragons from a fairy tale.

idTips.label: Tail Scales
idTips.description: Look for distinctive rows of large, sharp, spiny scales running along both edges of the tail - these feel rough and prickly to the touch, unlike the smooth tails of similar geckos

idTips.label: Color Change
idTips.description: Watch for dramatic color shifts from dark gray-brown with lighter spots in daylight to pale, almost translucent white at night - the transformation is quite striking

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small and delicate, about the length of your palm (4-5 inches total), with a slender build that feels surprisingly light and fragile when handled

idTips.label: Toe Pads
idTips.description: Notice the wide, sticky toe pads that feel slightly damp and rubbery - these allow them to climb up smooth glass windows and walls with ease

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Active at night around artificial lights, making soft chirping or clicking sounds, and freezing motionless when startled before darting away quickly

habitat: In New England, you'd only find this gecko indoors in heated buildings, as they cannot survive our cold winters outdoors. Look for them near warm areas like greenhouses, tropical plant shops, pet stores, or warehouses where they might have arrived accidentally in shipments. They prefer spots near lights where they can hunt flying insects.

seasonality.spring: Any sightings would be indoors in heated buildings, as they cannot survive New England's cool spring temperatures outside.
seasonality.summer: Might occasionally be spotted in very warm indoor spaces, but still cannot establish outdoor populations in New England's climate.
seasonality.fall: Indoor sightings only, if any, as outdoor temperatures quickly become too cold for survival.
seasonality.winter: Any observations would be strictly limited to heated indoor environments like greenhouses or tropical plant facilities.

funFact: This gecko can literally see in color at night! While most animals that are active in the dark have poor color vision, Indo-Pacific House Geckos have special color-detecting cells in their eyes that are 350 times more sensitive than human color vision, letting them see a rainbow world even in moonlight.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with the Mediterranean House Gecko, but the Indo-Pacific species has those telltale rows of large, spiny scales along the tail edges that feel rough to the touch. Memory trick: 'Indo-Pacific = spiny tail traffic lanes' - those spiny scale rows run like lanes down each side of the tail.
contextualKnowledge: This species is extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation, likely from an accidental introduction rather than an established population. Unlike some gecko species that can reproduce without males, these geckos need both sexes to breed, making it very unlikely they could establish permanent populations here even if they arrived regularly.
compareHints: Compared to its close cousin the Mediterranean House Gecko, the Indo-Pacific species has more pronounced spiny scales along the tail edges and tends to be slightly smaller overall. Both species can change color dramatically, but the Indo-Pacific gecko often becomes more translucent at night. The tropical House Gecko is more robust and lacks the distinctive spiny tail scale rows that make the Indo-Pacific species unique among house geckos.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mediterranean House Geckos are the most likely of the Hemidactylus genus to survive in New England's climate due to their cold tolerance and association with heated buildings.
The tropical house gecko is larger and more robust than its relative the Mediterranean house gecko, with a chunkier build and more pronounced toe pads.
